query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent Al2O3 coating on the surface of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures (800–1000 °C) without compromising its intrinsic room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin, adherent, high-temperature stable oxide coating (Al2O3) via vapor deposition or pack cementation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at temperatures between 800 and 1000 °C for a duration of 5 hours under strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal Al2O3 surface layer that adheres uniformly to the alloy.
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating acts as a diffusion barrier, preventing oxygen ingress and suppressing high-temperature oxidation (pesting) while leaving the bulk microstructure—and therefore mechanical properties—largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to exhibit markedly reduced surface oxidation and pesting under high-temperature exposure while retaining similar levels of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance and pesting under high-temperature exposure in an air atmosphere.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the temperature range of 800–1000 °C, exposure time of 5 hours in an air atmosphere, and under strain rates of 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1.
generation.uncertainty: Challenges include optimizing coating thickness and ensuring uniform adherence without affecting the bulk properties; long-term cyclic exposure effects and scale-up processes remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group with an Al2O3 coating applied via vapor deposition and a control group without any coating. Subject both groups to an air environment at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours, followed by mechanical testing (both tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C) and surface characterization (SEM, XRD analysis of oxidation products).
measurements: Thickness and morphology of the surface oxide layer
Visual assessment of pesting or degradation on sample surfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the coated samples do not demonstrate a significant reduction in oxidation (evidenced by similar oxide scale thickness and pesting as the control) or if the coating degrades the alloy's mechanical properties (reduced ductility or yield strength) relative to the untreated samples.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys in the Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr family focused on de‐convoluting mechanical performance through compositional tuning and processing methods. In parallel, a non‐equiatomic variant was shown to resist high‐temperature pesting via an oxidation-protection treatment—although that study did not test the equiatomic alloy. Over time, researchers have perfected bulk microstructure and strength (via subtraction techniques and thermomechanical processing) but have not yet translated these successes into reliable oxygen resistance for the equiatomic composition.
decision.unsolved: The outstanding challenge is to boost the oxygen resistance of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr at high temperatures (800–1000 °C) in air without altering its well-established room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength. In the equiatomic alloy, neither modified bulk composition approaches nor microstructural refinements have been shown to directly address oxidation-induced pesting.
decision.lever: apply a thin, adherent, high-temperature stable oxide coating (e.g., an Al2O3-based layer) via techniques such as vapor deposition or pack cementation
decision.why: A surface treatment confines the modification to the material’s outer region, preserving the high-performance bulk properties while providing a protective barrier against oxygen ingress. This strategy builds on prior oxidation-protection successes in related non-equiatomic alloys and matches the design constraint of a single intervention. A controlled experiment—comparing treated versus untreated samples exposed to air at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours under representative strain rates—with subsequent tensile testing would directly test whether the coating prevents pesting while maintaining the alloy’s ductility and yield strength. If the treated alloy fails to show reduced oxidation or if its mechanical performance is compromised, the hypothesis would be falsified.
